title: Va'era: too tired to hear (Exodus 6:9)
hook: the people can't listen "for impatience of spirit, and for cruel bondage"
tomorrow: Va'era: why Aaron struck the river

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'era: four promises, bring out, deliver, redeem, take, and four cups at the seder. Did you name a freedom before a sip? Today, Moses carries those promises to the people. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

You come home with great news. You found a better apartment, or a plan to fix the money problem, or a way out of the thing that's been dragging everyone down. You're excited. And the person you tell has just worked a double shift, the baby was up all night, and they barely look up. You say it again. Nothing. It's not that they don't care. They can't take it in. Moses has the best news in the world. God has promised freedom, four times over. He tells the people. And they don't listen.
screen: `THE BEST NEWS IN THE WORLD.` → `AFTER A DOUBLE SHIFT.` → `THEY DON'T LISTEN.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "but they hearkened not unto Moses for impatience of spirit, and for cruel bondage." The Hebrew for impatience of spirit is kotzer ruach. Literally, shortness of spirit, or shortness of breath. Ruach is both. Rashi pictures it physically: a person in distress whose breath comes short, who can't draw a long breath. Think of how you breathe when you're panicked or exhausted. Quick, shallow, high in the chest. There's no room in there for a new idea. And notice what the Torah doesn't do. It doesn't call the people faithless or stubborn. It gives the reason right there in the verse: cruel bondage. Hard labor. They're too crushed to hope. The text takes their side. Then Moses, discouraged, turns it on himself. If my own people won't listen to me, he says, how will Pharaoh? And God's answer is simply to send him back, with Aaron, to both. Again. The words don't change. The timing and the patience do. Later, when the people are free, they do hear. At the sea, the Torah says, they believed. Freedom came first. Listening came after. So when someone can't hear good news, or advice, or even love, the Torah suggests a different question. Not, why won't they listen? But, how short is their breath right now? What are they carrying? Sometimes the first job isn't to say it better. It's to lighten the load, and wait.
screen: `KOTZER RUACH — SHORT OF BREATH.` · `THE TORAH TAKES THEIR SIDE.` · `GO BACK AND SAY IT AGAIN.` · `FREEDOM FIRST, LISTENING AFTER.` · then, large: `TIRED EARS CAN'T HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with someone too tired to listen. Start with your own breath. Notice if it's short. Let it lengthen, slowly, a few times. Now think of someone who hasn't been hearing you lately. A partner, a parent, a coworker, a teenager. Ask what their bondage is right now: what hard labor are they under? Picture one way to lighten it before you try to be heard. The bell holds the time.
Va'era. The portion where the people can't hear Moses's good news, for shortness of spirit and cruel bondage.
Your line: tired ears can't hear. Today, when someone doesn't take something in, check how tired they are before you repeat yourself. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers often cite kotzer ruach when talking about burnout and poverty, and Jewish law places heavy weight on paying workers on time and not overburdening them, from the laws of wages and of the Sabbath rest.

myth: the Torah blames the people for not listening
it gives the reason in the same verse: shortness of spirit and cruel bondage.
ruach can mean both spirit and breath
so kotzer ruach is shortness of spirit and shortness of breath.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you brought the people God's promise of freedom, and they were too crushed to listen. what now?
options: wait until they come to you.
fork.reveal: Moses was discouraged, but God sent him back, with Aaron, to the people and to Pharaoh. later, at the sea, the people believed.

original.note: Hebrew: shortness of spirit, shortness of breath (Exodus 6:9).

trapdoor: what you thought: the people didn't have enough faith.
what it means: they were too exhausted by slavery to take in good news.
what a scholar hears: Rashi reads kotzer ruach physically, as the short breath of someone in distress, since ruach is both spirit and breath.
